newsitem.title: UK: S&P rates Croatia BBB minus l-term foreign crncy.
newsitem.headline: S&P rates Croatia BBB minus l-term foreign crncy.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Friday it had assigned its BBB minus long-term and A3 short-term foreign currency ratings to the Republic of Croatia.

S&P also said it had assigned its A minus long-term and A2 short-term local currency ratings to the republic, affecting about Croatian kuna 200 million (US$37 million) of kuna- denominated treasury bills and the recent 300 million kuna Eurobond.
"The outlook on the long-term ratings is stable," S&P said in a statement.
The rating agecny said Croatia's ratings were supported by:
-- The government's commitment to orthodox economic policies, which have reduced inflation to modest levels (three percent in 1996) from hyper-inflation as recently as 1993.
-- Robust public finances, with the general government deficit likely to remain at three percent of GDP this year and net public external debt equal to just three percent of exports in 1996.
-- very low external debt service (including short-term debt) equivalent to 15 percent of exports in 1996 compared with that of similarly-rated sovereigns.
-- Improving economic prospects. GDP grew by 6% last year, reflecting a revival in industrial output and tourism, as well as strong consumer demand.
-- Increasing economic integration with Europe, improving ties with its neighbors, and the stabilization of the security situation in Bosnia.
But S&P said the ratings were constrained by the challenges of:
-- maintaining fiscal restraint while rebuilding the war-damaged country and accelerating structural reforms in the banking and corporate sectors.
-- Developing a still nascent democratic culture and strengthening democratic institutions in response to the population's demands for greater political freedom.

-- Containing the large current account deficit (10 percent of GDP in 1996), driven by reconstruction and economic restructuring, by strengthening the country's traditionally good export and tourism base.
"Croatia's ratings depend on continued adherence to conservative fiscal policies and progress in restructuring the banking and corporate sectors," S&P said.

"The mid-year 1997 presidential elections and succession concerns related to uncertainties about the President's health are unlikely to threaten either Croatia's political maturation, or its commitment to reform and prudent economic management."
The agency said that diplomatic pressure from NATO and the U.N. should help strengthen the region's stability and underpin Croatia's continued economic recovery.
"Looking ahead, maintaining low inflation, sustaining output growth and reviving employment, are the key economic challenges, the statement added.
